messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Workplace: Workplace, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 55-year-old African American man who has worked for years as a house painter, moving from room to room with a radio on low and the smell of primer and thinner in the air. He came to treatment after the sudden death of a loved one, a loss that had split his life into a clear before and after. The death had unfolded in an emergency setting, and what remains most searing is not a calm narrative but flashes: the ambulance lights, the sound of urgent voices, the sense that everything was happening too fast while he could do nothing to stop it. Even now, when he tries to speak about that day, he does not always get a full scene. Sometimes the feeling arrives first and all at once—raw grief and panic with no clear picture attached—and at other times what comes are stark visual fragments, like still photographs he cannot control.

In the weeks after the death, ordinary parts of life began to take on the charge of that day. Seeing an ambulance on the street could make his whole body tighten before he had even fully registered what he was looking at. At work, being on a job site became difficult in ways that embarrassed him. If a coworker mentioned someone who had lost a spouse, parent, or child, Kwame would go quiet and feel himself leave the conversation internally, as if he were already back in the emotional weather of the loss. The workplace itself became a setting he dreaded; climbing ladders and painting trim in clients’ homes, he found himself listening for sirens outside and scanning for signs that something terrible was about to happen. Those moments did more than upset him. They left him feeling that his life had been shattered beyond repair, and that other people were still moving through an intact world from which he had been cut off.

As these reactions persisted, Kwame had come to believe that he was no longer the man he had been before. He described feeling as if he did not know himself anymore: a man who used to work steadily, talk easily, and return home tired but settled now moved through his days braced and estranged. That sense of being altered fed his watchfulness. He was certain something in him had changed permanently, and because of that he no longer trusted his surroundings, even in his own house. Nights were the worst. Daylight offered distraction, but after dark he felt exposed, tense, and unable to let down his guard. He checked doors, listened for sounds outside, and stayed keyed up long after his wife had gone to bed.

His view of himself and his life also shaped the way the loss stayed in his mind. Because he saw the event as having destroyed his life, any return of memory seemed to confirm it. When images surfaced, they were not just recollections; they felt like proof that he was trapped in the worst moment of his life. And when no image came, only the same crushing emotional force, that too reinforced his sense that the loss had taken over from the inside, beyond his control. The more isolated he felt from others, the less likely he was to talk, and the less he talked, the more the memories remained unprocessed, returning as pictures, surges of grief, or sudden emotional collapses without warning.

A tightening pattern gradually took hold. When Kwame felt on guard at home or caught himself tensing at night, the heightened alertness itself seemed to pull the trauma closer. In that state, his mind became quick to latch onto ambulance sirens in the distance, conversations about bereavement, or reminders at work that might otherwise have passed him by. Once activated, those cues brought back the images and the unbearable grief, and the memories in turn made his body feel even more ready for danger. After a bad night he would go to work already braced, and because he was scanning so hard for threat, the workplace felt full of reminders. By the end of the day he would think, again, that this was all his life was now: a man set apart, a man ruined by what happened.

Over time he withdrew socially, not because he had lost interest in people in a general way, but because talk of illness, death, or family emergencies had become so potent that he could not stay present for it. His wife noticed he was harder to reach and more restless after dark. He began to fear not only the memories themselves but the places and moments that might call them up, and the more that happened, the more convinced he became that nowhere was truly safe. He finally sought help when he realized he was dreading both home at night and the job sites where he had spent most of his adult life. What frightens him most is the thought that the loss has permanently destroyed who he is. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he might learn how to be in his own home, hear an ambulance, or stand at work without feeling pulled back into that day.
